{"request_id":"663c2e66ed5c2e66ed5cba38d17dc0bc","rewritten_text":"These deputies had been sent by their respective parties to Adrian, who had been chosen as arbiter; they had travelled from Paris to Calais through empty towns and a desolated land, cherishing meanwhile a fierce hatred of one another; and now they urged their separate claims with unabated party zeal.

By questioning the deputies separately, and after long inquiry, we discovered the real condition of affairs at Paris. Ever since parliament had named him Ryland’s deputy, all the surviving English had yielded obedience to Adrian. He was our captain, to conduct us from our native land to regions unknown; our legislator and our guardian. When our plan of emigration was first arranged, no lasting division among our members had been intended, and the authority over the entire body, rising by degrees, culminated in the Earl of Windsor. Yet unforeseen events altered our designs, and caused the larger portion of our people to be separated from their supreme leader for nearly two months. They had crossed in two distinct companies; and, upon reaching Paris, discord sprang up between them.

They found Paris deserted. When the plague first showed itself, returning travellers and merchants, together with letters, kept us regularly informed of the havoc wrought by disease upon the continent. But as mortality increased, this intercourse diminished and at last ceased. Even within England, communication between one part of the island and another became tardy and infrequent. No ship crossed the waters dividing Calais from Dover; or, if some sorrowful voyager, eager to learn whether his kindred lived or died, set out from the French coast to return to us, the ravenous sea often engulfed his frail vessel, or, after a day or two, he caught the disease and died before he could relate the tale of France’s desolation. Thus we remained, in great measure, ignorant of the continent’s condition, and retained some indistinct hope of finding many companions across its broad expanse. But the same causes which had so dreadfully reduced the English nation had found still wider room for destruction in the sister country. France was a void; along the long road from Calais to Paris, not a single human being appeared. In Paris there were a few—perhaps a hundred—who, resigned to their approaching doom, wandered through the capital’s streets and gathered to speak of former days, with that liveliness, even gaiety, which rarely abandons the people of that nation.

The English entered into undisputed possession of Paris. Its lofty houses and confined streets were without life. A few wan figures could be seen at the familiar gathering-place in the Tuileries; they marvelled why the islanders had come near their doomed city—for in the extremity of misery, sufferers always suppose their own share of calamity the most bitter, just as, under acute pain, we would trade the particular torment beneath which we writhe for any other that might afflict another part of the body."}

{"request_id":"e6adf23cee745da69e6e6a67","rewritten_text":"This marriage is entirely right. I did not think so at first, but I admit it now. The gods made Sibyl Vane for you. Without her, you would have been incomplete.”

“Thank you, Basil,” Dorian Gray replied, squeezing his hand. “I knew you would understand me. Harry is so cynical; he frightens me. But here is the orchestra. It is terrible, though it lasts only about five minutes. Then the curtain will rise, and you will see the girl to whom I am going to give my whole life, to whom I have given everything good in me.”

A quarter of an hour later, amid a remarkable storm of applause, Sibyl Vane came onto the stage. Yes, she was certainly beautiful—one of the most beautiful creatures Lord Henry had ever seen. There was something of a young deer in her shy grace and startled eyes. A light blush, like the reflection of a rose in a silver mirror, rose in her cheeks as she looked at the crowded, excited audience. She stepped back a few paces, and her lips seemed to tremble. Basil Hallward sprang to his feet and began to clap. Dorian Gray sat still, as if dreaming, watching her. Lord Henry looked through his glasses and murmured, “Charming! Charming!”

The scene was the hall in Capulet’s house. Romeo, dressed as a pilgrim, had entered with Mercutio and his other friends. The band, poor as it was, played a few bars of music, and the dance began. Among the awkward, badly dressed actors, Sibyl Vane moved like a being from a better world. As she danced, her body swayed like a plant moving in water. The shape of her throat was like that of a white lily. Her hands seemed formed from cool ivory.

Yet she was strangely lifeless. When her eyes fell on Romeo, she showed no joy. The few lines she had to speak—

Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much, Which mannerly devotion shows in this; For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do touch, And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss—

{"request_id":"c49ed6e0600175082355e75d","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” I said, “what is wrong now? How is your master?”

“Why, to tell de truth, massa, he not as well as he might be.”

“Not well! I am very sorry to hear it. What does he complain of?”

“Dat’s just it! He never complains of nothin’—but he berry sick all de same.”

“Very sick, Jupiter! Why didn’t you say so right away? Is he in bed?”

“No, he ain’t! He ain’t settled nowhere—that’s what troubles me. My mind is berry heavy about poor Massa Will.”

“Jupiter, I would like to understand what you mean. You say your master is ill. Hasn’t he told you what is wrong with him?”

“Why, massa, it ain’t no use getting angry about it—Massa Will says nothin’ at all is wrong with him—but what makes him walk around like dis, with his head down and his shoulders up, white as a goose? And then he keeps a cipher all de time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“Keeps a cipher with figures on a slate—the strangest figures I ever did see. I’m getting scared, I tell you. I have to keep a mighty close eye on him all de time. The other day he slipped away before sunrise and was gone the whole blessed day. I had a big stick cut, ready to give him a terrible beating when he came back—but I’m such a fool I hadn’t the heart after all—he looked so very poorly.”

“Eh? What? Ah, yes! On the whole, I think you had better not be too hard on the poor fellow—don’t whip him, Jupiter—he can hardly bear it. But can you think of what caused this illness, or rather this change in his behavior? Has anything unpleasant happened since I saw you?”

“No, massa, nothing unpleasant happened since then—it was before then I’m afraid—it was the very day you were there.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Why, massa, I mean de bug—there now.”

“The what?”

“De bug. I’m berry certain Massa Will was bitten somewhere around de head by dat gold-bug.”

“And what reason do you have, Jupiter, for thinking that?”

“Claws enough, massa, and a mouth too. I never saw such a wicked bug—he kicks and bites everything that comes near him. Massa Will caught him first, but had to let him go again mighty quick, I tell you—then was when he must have got bitten. “Thank you, Basil,” Dorian Gray replied, squeezing his hand. “I knew you would understand me. Harry is so cynical; he frightens me. But here is the orchestra. It is dreadful, really, though it lasts only about five minutes. Then the curtain will rise, and you will see the girl to whom I am going to give my whole life, to whom I have given everything good in me.”

A quarter of an hour later, amid an extraordinary storm of applause, Sibyl Vane came onto the stage. Yes, she was certainly beautiful—one of the most beautiful creatures Lord Henry thought he had ever seen. There was something fawnlike in her shy grace and startled eyes. A faint blush, like the reflection of a rose in a silver mirror, rose in her cheeks as she looked at the crowded, enthusiastic audience. She stepped back a few paces, and her lips seemed to tremble. Basil Hallward sprang to his feet and began applauding. Dorian Gray sat motionless, as if dreaming, watching her. Lord Henry looked through his glasses and murmured, “Charming! Charming!”

The scene was the hall in Capulet’s house, and Romeo, dressed as a pilgrim, had entered with Mercutio and his other friends. The band, such as it was, played a few bars of music, and the dance began. Among the clumsy, shabbily dressed actors, Sibyl Vane moved like a being from a finer world. As she danced, her body swayed like a plant in water. The lines of her throat were like those of a white lily. Her hands seemed formed of cool ivory.

Yet she was strangely lifeless. She showed no joy when her eyes fell on Romeo. The few lines she had to speak—
